title: Load a new lancet into a pen lancing device: cap off, lancet in, tab twisted off, cap snapped back on, device cocked
instruction: Load the new lancet into the lancing device: take the device's end cap off, push the lancet into the holder, twist off the lancet's protective tab, put the end cap back on, then cock the device by pulling its arming barrel back until it clicks. Lay the device down on the table.
context: Why it matters (assistive care): 589 million adults have diabetes (IDF Diabetes Atlas, 2024); in the US, 38.4 million people, 16.5 million of them aged 65 or over (CDC). A fingerstick glucose check needs a fresh lancet in the person's own pen lancing device. CDC: "Never use fingerstick devices for more than one person" (hepatitis B has spread among people having their glucose monitored in long-term care), so a helper cannot bring one ready loaded. Loading is small work with a needle in it. People with memory loss often cannot self-test reliably and carers take it over; poor sight and numb or shaky fingers make the same step hard. A robot that loads the lancet keeps the test in the person's own hands. Left unsaid by the instruction: no step works one-handed (the 29 g device slides at 0.17 N; its cap snaps on with 2 N, its barrel pulls 1.3 N), the tab must be twisted (its neck stands an 8 N pull), and a gripper that touches the bare needle scores 0.
setup: Positions in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases, on the table (x forward, y left). Lancing device: pen-shaped, 13.4 cm long with its cap on, 29 g in all, lying along y with its nose toward the right arm, the tip of its nose at x 34, y 5 (layout A) or x 32.5, y 6.5 (layout B, environment variable LANCET_LOT=B). Body: blue plastic, 17 mm across, 7.8 cm long, 22 g, with an 8 mm flat it lies on and a yellow trigger button on top; at its front a dark grey nose 9 mm across and 12 mm long with the lancet holder in it, a round socket 4.8 mm across and 9 mm deep with a rounded mouth, which grips a lancet pushed to within 1 mm of its floor and lets go at a 2.5 N pull. End cap: pale grey plastic, 17 mm across, 3.4 cm long, 3 g; it fits over the nose and snaps against the body's shoulder (lets go at a 2 N pull); it starts on. Arming barrel: dark grey plastic, 17 mm across, 2.2 cm long, 4 g, on the body's rear end; it slides back 8 mm against a return spring (200 N/m) and cocks the device at 6.5 mm. Lancet: one twist-top lancet, 3.25 cm long with its tab, 0.6 g: a white round plastic body 4 mm across and 2.45 cm long with a rounded insertion end, a 3 mm needle at the other end, and over the needle a white protective tab 6.4 mm across and 8 mm long on a moulded neck (twists off at 0.004 N m after an eighth of a turn; stands an 8 N pull). It lies along y on the kit tray's ridge, its insertion end toward the device at x 21.8, y -14.8, its axis 3.2 cm above the table. Kit tray: grey plastic block 7 x 11 x 2 cm fixed to the table, middle at x 24, y -16, with a ridge 8 mm wide, 1.9 cm long and 1 cm tall with two 1.5 mm kerbs under the lancet (the tab overhangs its end) and two rails 6 cm long, 2.5 mm tall and 1.1 cm apart as a cradle for the cap. Dish: open white plastic dish, 7 cm across inside, 2 cm tall, 30 g, loose, base centred at x 44, y -1, for the tab. Both arms start in the raised ready pose, grippers open.
scoring: Tools: a close video of the device, a ruler, a protractor or level. 0 if at the end the lancet is not home in the holder (home: its insertion end within 1 mm of the socket's floor, inside the socket and within 10 degrees of in line, so 15.5 mm of its body stands out of the nose; out again once drawn back 3 mm); or if at any time while the tab was off and taken 10 mm clear of the lancet and the end cap was not snapped on, any part of a gripper came within 2 mm of the needle; or if the device went off the table. Otherwise 0.25: the lancet is home with its tab still on. 0.5: the tab is off (its neck has let go: twisted 45 degrees or more, or forced more than 4 mm or 20 degrees out of place; the tab is a separate piece). 0.75: and at the end the end cap is snapped on (its mouth within 1 mm of the body's shoulder, round the nose and within 10 degrees of in line; off again once drawn back 3 mm). 1.0: and the device has been cocked (its arming barrel pulled back 6.5 mm or more at some time in the trial), it lies on the table within 5 degrees of level with its underside within 2 mm of the surface, the device, cap, barrel and lancet are at rest (under 2 cm/s), and no part of either gripper is within 3 cm of the device.
reset_notes: Each trial uses up one lancet. Take the cap off, pull the used lancet out into a sharps container, refit the cap, press the trigger to release the spring and lay the device on its marks. Put a new lancet on the tray's ridge with its tab toward the robot's right, and empty the dish. To keep a failed trial from puncturing a gripper pad, use lancets whose needle has been blunted, or fit thin puncture-resistant covers over the pads; touching the needle is still scored from the video.
fidelity: Body, barrel, cap, lancet and tab are loose rigid bodies; the barrel rides a sprung slide. The cap's snap (2 N), the holder's grip (2.5 N), the neck (0.004 N m, off at 45 degrees) and the spring (200 N/m) are estimates sized to the robot's 3 N, not measurements. Round lancet (real ones have a square end); cap bore 2.2 mm over a slick, round-edged nose; needle drawn, touching judged by distance; not fired. Lancet size from a listed 30G twist lancet; device sizes typical, not one model.
scores: Dream-1 run: 0.0 (left gripper lifted the device by its body, right came up to the cap but never drew it off; device put back capped, lancet not taken); demo: 1.0 (layout A, full score at step 1,729; layout B also 1.0). Videos: overhead, right wrist and left wrist cameras side by side.
